_comment: Adversarial benchmark. Fully synthetic — no real patients, no real clinicians. Each case has a transcript (ground truth conversation), a note_under_test (what an ambient scribe supposedly produced), and ground_truth describing any deliberately injected error. Expanded from a 6-case starter set to 18: 3 numeric_medication_error, 3 fabrication, 3 negation_error, 2 distortion, 2 misattribution, 2 omission, 3 clean controls (no planted error, used to measure false-positive rate). The omission category was added once the pipeline actually gained a way to detect it (see src/pipeline.py's omission_check_batch) — before that, planting omission cases would have scored 0% against a detector that didn't exist.

cases.transcript:
Doctor: Hi Mr. Alvarez, good to see you. How have you been feeling since we adjusted your blood pressure medication?
Patient: Pretty good, actually. No headaches or dizziness like before.
Doctor: That's great. Are you still taking the lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day?
Patient: Yes, every morning with breakfast.
Doctor: Any side effects, cough, swelling in your legs?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Let's check your blood pressure today... okay, it's reading 128 over 82. That's a nice improvement from last visit.
Patient: That's good to hear.
Doctor: I want you to keep taking the lisinopril at the same dose and come back in three months for a recheck.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports feeling well since blood pressure medication adjustment. Denies headaches, dizziness, cough, or leg swelling. Taking lisinopril 20mg once daily each morning with breakfast.
Objective: Blood pressure 128/82, improved from previous visit.
Assessment: Hypertension, well-controlled on current regimen.
Plan: Continue lisinopril at current dose. Return to clinic in 3 months for recheck.

injected_errors.transcript_evidence: Patient confirmed 'lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day'

cases.transcript:
Doctor: What brings you in today?
Patient: I've had this cough for about five days now, kind of a dry cough. No fever that I've noticed.
Doctor: Any shortness of breath, chest pain, or sore throat?
Patient: A little bit of a sore throat, but no chest pain or trouble breathing.
Doctor: Any nausea, vomiting, or stomach issues?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Okay, let me listen to your lungs... they sound clear. Your throat looks a little red but no white patches. I think this is a viral upper respiratory infection.
Patient: Okay, so nothing serious?
Doctor: No, should resolve on its own. Drink plenty of fluids, rest, and use over-the-counter cough drops as needed. Come back if it gets worse or lasts more than two weeks.
Patient: Will do, thank you.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports a dry cough for 5 days, accompanied by fever and mild nausea. Also endorses mild sore throat. Denies chest pain or shortness of breath.
Objective: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. Oropharynx mildly erythematous, no exudate.
Assessment: Viral upper respiratory infection.
Plan: Supportive care - fluids, rest, OTC cough drops as needed. Return if symptoms worsen or persist beyond 2 weeks.

injected_errors.claim_text: accompanied by fever and mild nausea
injected_errors.correct_value: not mentioned; patient explicitly denied fever and denied nausea/vomiting
injected_errors.transcript_evidence: Patient said 'No fever that I've noticed' and, on nausea/vomiting, 'No, none of that.'

Doctor: Tell me about this back pain you've been having.
Patient: It's been about a week, lower back, mostly on the right side. It's a dull ache, gets worse when I bend over.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling down your legs?
Patient: No, I don't have any numbness or tingling. Just the ache in my back.
Doctor: Any weakness in your legs, or problems with your bladder or bowels?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Did anything specific cause it, heavy lifting, a fall?
Patient: I did move some furniture last weekend, so maybe that.
Doctor: Okay, this sounds like a musculoskeletal strain. Let's start with ibuprofen as needed, apply heat, and avoid heavy lifting for the next week or two.
Patient: Okay, I can do that.
Doctor: If you develop any numbness, weakness, or bladder or bowel problems, come in right away or go to the ER.
Patient: Understood.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports 1 week of dull, lower back pain, right-sided, worse with bending. Reports numbness and tingling radiating into the legs. Denies bladder or bowel dysfunction. Likely related to lifting furniture last weekend.
Objective: Not specified during this encounter.
Assessment: Musculoskeletal low back strain.
Plan: Ibuprofen as needed, heat application, avoid heavy lifting 1-2 weeks. Return or seek emergency care if numbness, weakness, or bladder/bowel symptoms develop.

injected_errors.claim_text: Reports numbness and tingling radiating into the legs
injected_errors.transcript_evidence: Patient said 'No, I don't have any numbness or tingling.'

cases.transcript:
Doctor: How's your blood sugar control been since your last visit?
Patient: Pretty good overall. I did have one episode of feeling really shaky and sweaty about two weeks ago, maybe thirty minutes after I skipped lunch.
Doctor: Did you check your blood sugar at the time?
Patient: Yeah, it was 58.
Doctor: Okay, that's a mild low. Has that happened more than once?
Patient: No, just that one time.
Doctor: Any other episodes of highs or lows?
Patient: No, otherwise it's been pretty steady, mostly in the 100 to 140 range.
Doctor: Good. Let's keep the metformin dose the same, and I want you to make sure you don't skip meals, especially lunch.
Patient: Okay, I'll be more careful about that.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports recurring episodes of hypoglycemia over the past two weeks, with symptoms of shakiness and sweating, occurring several times, most recently associated with skipping lunch. Blood glucose checked during one episode was 58 mg/dL. Otherwise blood glucose readings have ranged 100-140.
Objective: Not specified during this encounter.
Assessment: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, recurrent mild hypoglycemia.
Plan: Continue metformin at current dose. Counseled patient on avoiding skipped meals.

injected_errors.claim_text: recurring episodes of hypoglycemia ... occurring several times
injected_errors.transcript_evidence: Patient said 'just that one time' when asked if it happened more than once

cases.specialty: Primary care - sore throat / strep pharyngitis
cases.transcript:
Doctor: What's going on today?
Patient: My throat has been really sore for the past three days, and it hurts to swallow.
Doctor: Any fever, cough, or runny nose?
Patient: I had a low fever yesterday, around 100.4, but no cough or runny nose.
Doctor: Any swollen glands or rash?
Patient: My neck feels a little swollen and tender on both sides.
Doctor: Let me take a look... your tonsils are swollen and red with some white patches. I'm going to do a rapid strep test.
Doctor: The rapid strep test came back positive. I'm going to prescribe amoxicillin, 500 milligrams, twice a day for 10 days.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
Doctor: Make sure you finish the whole course even if you start feeling better. Use ibuprofen or acetaminophen for pain and fever as needed. Come back if you're not improving in 2-3 days after starting the antibiotic.
Patient: Will do.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports 3 days of sore throat with pain on swallowing. Reports subjective fever of 100.4F yesterday. Denies cough or rhinorrhea. Reports bilateral tender cervical lymphadenopathy.
Objective: Tonsils erythematous and enlarged with white exudate. Rapid strep test positive.
Assessment: Streptococcal pharyngitis.
Plan: Amoxicillin 500mg twice daily for 10 days, counseled to complete full course. Ibuprofen or acetaminophen as needed for pain/fever. Return if not improving in 2-3 days.

cases.transcript:
Doctor: Let's take a look at his ears... yes, the right eardrum is red and bulging, that's consistent with an ear infection.
Parent: Oh no, poor guy. Does he need antibiotics?
Doctor: Yes, I'll prescribe amoxicillin. For his weight, that's going to be 250 milligrams, three times a day, for 10 days.
Parent: Okay, three times a day for 10 days. Should I give it with food?
Doctor: Either way is fine, whatever's easier for him to take.
Parent: Any side effects to watch for?
Doctor: Mainly loose stools or a mild rash - if you see a rash that looks like hives, stop it and call us right away.
Parent: Understood. Anything else?
Doctor: Use children's ibuprofen or acetaminophen for the ear pain as needed. Follow up in 2 weeks, sooner if he's not improving in 48-72 hours.
Parent: Thank you.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Parent reports concern for ear pain. Objective: Right tympanic membrane erythematous and bulging, consistent with acute otitis media.
Assessment: Acute otitis media, right ear.
Plan: Amoxicillin 500mg three times daily for 10 days. Counseled on side effects (loose stools, rash - discontinue and call if hives develop). Children's ibuprofen or acetaminophen as needed for pain. Follow up in 2 weeks, sooner if not improving in 48-72 hours.

injected_errors.transcript_evidence: Doctor said 'that's going to be 250 milligrams, three times a day'

Patient: Yes, morning and evening.
Doctor: Good, any dizziness or fainting spells?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Let's stick with the same dose for now and recheck in a month. If the tiredness gets worse, call us.

Assessment: Atrial fibrillation, rate-controlled on current beta blocker.
Plan: Continue metoprolol 50mg twice daily. Recheck in 1 month; call if fatigue worsens.

Doctor: Tell me about this knee pain.
Patient: It's my right knee, been bothering me for about two weeks, mostly when I go up and down stairs.
Doctor: Any swelling that you've noticed, or does it feel warm?
Patient: No swelling that I've seen, and it doesn't feel warm or anything.
Doctor: Let me examine it... range of motion looks good, no instability, no tenderness along the joint line. I think this is likely patellofemoral pain, pretty common with stair use.
Patient: Okay, what should I do?
Doctor: Ice after activity, and I'll give you some exercises to strengthen the muscles around the knee. Avoid stairs when you can for the next couple weeks.
Patient: Got it, thanks.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports 2 weeks of right knee pain, worse with stairs. Denies warmth.
Objective: Notable right knee swelling on exam. Range of motion intact, no instability, no joint line tenderness.
Assessment: Patellofemoral pain syndrome, right knee.
Plan: Ice after activity, home strengthening exercises, avoid stairs when possible for 2 weeks.

injected_errors.correct_value: not mentioned; patient explicitly denied noticing any swelling

cases.specialty: Primary care - hypertension follow-up, medication reconciliation
cases.transcript:
Doctor: Let's go over your medications. Still just the lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day?
Patient: Yes, that's the only prescription. Oh, I've also been taking ibuprofen fairly often, maybe every other day, for headaches.
Doctor: How often is 'fairly often' - like how many days a week?
Patient: Probably 3 to 4 days a week, over the counter, 200 milligram tablets.
Doctor: Okay, that's actually important to know, ibuprofen can interact with your blood pressure medication and affect your kidneys with regular use. Let's talk about alternatives for the headaches.
Patient: Oh, I didn't realize that.
Doctor: Try acetaminophen instead for now, and let's see if the headaches improve. If they continue, we should investigate the headaches themselves.
Patient: Okay, I can do that.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient continues lisinopril 10mg once daily for hypertension, no side effects reported.
Objective: Not specified during this encounter.
Assessment: Hypertension, stable on current regimen.
Plan: Continue lisinopril as prescribed. Follow up as scheduled.

injected_errors.claim_text: regular OTC ibuprofen use (3-4 days/week) for headaches, and the counseling to switch to acetaminophen given the interaction risk with lisinopril
injected_errors.correct_value: the note should document the ibuprofen use, the interaction discussion, and the plan to switch to acetaminophen
injected_errors.transcript_evidence: Patient reported taking ibuprofen '3 to 4 days a week' and the doctor said it 'can interact with your blood pressure medication' and recommended switching to acetaminophen

cases.transcript:
Doctor: What brings you in today?
Patient: I have a mole on my back that my partner noticed looks a little different lately.
Doctor: Different how - has it changed in size, color, or shape?
Patient: A bit darker maybe, and possibly a little bigger, over the last couple months.
Doctor: Any itching, bleeding, or pain from it?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Let me take a look... it's about 6 millimeters, mostly even in color and border, but given the changes you're describing I'd like to do a biopsy just to be safe.
Patient: Okay, that sounds reasonable.
Doctor: We'll do that today, it's a quick procedure, and I'll have you back in 2 weeks for the results.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports a back mole noted by partner to have darkened and possibly enlarged over the past 2 months. Denies itching, bleeding, or pain from the lesion.
Objective: Approximately 6mm pigmented lesion, generally even color and border on exam.
Assessment: Atypical-appearing nevus given reported change, biopsy indicated to rule out malignancy.
Plan: Shave biopsy performed today. Follow up in 2 weeks for results.

cases.specialty: Primary care - annual physical, no complaints
cases.transcript:
Doctor: How have you been feeling overall this year?
Patient: Really good, no complaints. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, sleeping well, eating well.
Doctor: Any changes in weight, appetite, or energy levels?
Patient: No, everything's been pretty stable.
Doctor: Great. Let's do a quick exam... heart and lungs sound normal, abdomen is soft and non-tender, everything looks good.
Patient: Glad to hear it.
Doctor: I'll order your routine annual labs - cholesterol panel and basic metabolic panel. Keep up with the exercise and diet, and I'll see you again next year unless something comes up sooner.
Patient: Will do, thank you.
cases.note_under_test:
Subjective: Patient reports feeling well overall, no complaints. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or changes in weight, appetite, sleep, or energy.
Objective: Heart and lungs normal on auscultation. Abdomen soft, non-tender.
Assessment: Routine annual physical, no acute concerns.
Plan: Routine annual labs ordered (lipid panel, basic metabolic panel). Continue current diet and exercise. Follow up in 1 year or sooner if needed.
